videos.title: UK warns Iran's Hormuz blockade could trigger global food crisis

moments.quote: Britain is warning that the war on Iran could soon develop into a global food crisis.
moments.why: The journalist explicitly mentions the risk of a global food crisis due to the conflict with Iran.

moments.quote: They say that the damage from the delays is already being priced into the agricultural markets, raising fears of lower harvest and rising food costs.
moments.why: The journalist reports on the economic impact of the conflict on food prices and harvests.

moments.quote: The World Food Programme estimates that some 45 million more people could fall into acute food insecurity if the conflict continues.
moments.why: The journalist cites the World Food Programme's warning about food insecurity linked to the conflict.

moments.quote: The world risks sleepwalking into a global food crisis, and we cannot risk tens of millions of people going hungry because Iran has hijacked an international shipping lane.
moments.why: The UK Foreign Secretary explicitly warns of a global food crisis and mass hunger due to Iran's actions.

videos.title: Could Iran war trigger a hunger crisis? | Counting the Cost

moments.quote: Food prices are up and fertilizer costs are soaring. Aid agencies are calling for the free flow of commodities through the Strait of Hormuz. But could supplies be rerouted and at what cost? The UN warns 45 million more people could face hunger as the Iran conflict drags on. So is the world headed toward another hunger crisis or could it soon be averted?
moments.why: The journalist explicitly mentions the risk of a hunger crisis due to the Iran conflict and rising food prices.

moments.quote: The next global food crisis may not begin in farms or supermarkets. It's unfolding in a narrow stretch of water. The UN warns if fertilizers cannot pass through the Strait of Hormuz in the next few weeks, the world could face mass starvation. It says the consequences could be severe if shipping disruptions linked to the Iran conflict drag on. Food prices are already at a three-year high while fertilizer costs critical for agriculture have surged. Aid agencies fear a prolonged disruption could push tens of millions more people into hunger.
moments.why: The journalist details the UN's warning about mass starvation and a global food crisis linked to the Iran conflict.

moments.quote: World food prices are at a three-year high as the Iran war sends shockwaves through global markets. A United Nations report says the cost of basic essentials rose 1.6% in April. A lot of that is being driven by vegetable oil, which jumped nearly 6%. Meat prices rose 1.2% and cereals are up just under 1%. Overall, global food prices are now 2.5% higher than they were just one year ago.
moments.why: The reporter links the Iran war to rising global food prices and a potential food insecurity crisis.

moments.quote: But the long-term danger comes from fertilizer shortages. Around one-third of the world's supply also comes from the Gulf. Prices are on the rise, further squeezing margins for farmers. The cost and availability of fertilizer will seriously impact how much food they end up producing.
moments.why: The reporter explains how fertilizer shortages from the Gulf conflict could lead to reduced food production and crisis.

moments.quote: Planting season ends in some African countries in May, in others it's in June, others it's July and then it's August. And basically we have a few weeks ahead of us to prevent what will likely be a massive humanitarian crisis. We may be witnessing a crisis that will force 45 million more people into hunger and starvation.
moments.why: An official from the UN Office for Project Services warns of a massive humanitarian crisis and starvation due to the conflict's impact on agriculture.

moments.quote: Countries already struggling with conflict, food shortages, and economic shocks could be pushed over the edge. International agencies are warning against hoarding vital supplies and are urging provision for those who are most at risk.
moments.why: The reporter highlights the risk of countries being pushed into severe food shortages due to the conflict.

moments.quote: Short of actually having the Strait of Hormuz reopened, is there anything that the world can do at this stage to prevent this? What needs to be done short of reopening the Strait of Hormuz is shoring up the social protection systems in fragile countries. The countries that are already experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, the countries that are the most fragile... need to get support to support their population from experiencing the most severe impacts from this situation.
moments.why: The WFP official discusses measures to prevent the severe impacts of food insecurity caused by the conflict.

moments.quote: We're talking about this horrifying statistic of potentially 45 million more people around the globe potentially being pushed into hunger or starvation. Where is it likely that we are going to see this most acutely? It's based on a scenario of the barrel of oil staying above $100 until the end of June... Asia and East Africa were the two places in the world that would be most affected.
moments.why: The WFP official confirms the risk of 45 million people facing hunger due to the economic impacts of the war.

moments.quote: Already they're struggling with the cost of inputs. Cost of seeds, cost of fertilizer, herbicides, and pesticides have also increased. Ahmed Idris, Al Jazeera, for Counting the Cost in Abuja, Nigeria.
moments.why: The reporter links the Iran war to rising agricultural costs in Nigeria, contributing to food insecurity.

videos.title: Why the world could be heading for a wheat crisis

moments.quote: You could soon be paying a lot more for a loaf of bread. The UN's food security experts say the combination of the war in Iran, Ukraine and climate change have created a perfect storm for wheat.
moments.why: The journalist explicitly mentions the UN's food security experts' warning about a 'perfect storm' for wheat due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

videos.title: Could Iran war trigger the next global food shock? | Counting the Cost

moments.quote: Could this conflict trigger the next global food shock?
moments.why: Le présentateur évoque explicitement le risque d'un choc alimentaire mondial lié au conflit.

moments.quote: The United Nation warns rising food, oil and shipping costs could push an additional 45 million people into acute hunger, taking the global total above its record at 319 million. Could the Middle East conflict trigger the next global food shock
moments.why: Le journaliste cite un avertissement des Nations Unies concernant la menace imminente de famine et de faim aiguë liée au conflit.

moments.quote: The spike in global food and fuel costs could leave millions of families priced out of stable foods, particularly in import dependent countries like sub Saharan Africa and Asia.
moments.why: Un responsable du Programme alimentaire mondial met en garde contre l'augmentation des coûts alimentaires mondiaux et le risque de famine pour des millions de familles.

moments.quote: I think the obviously the most vulnerable is within the Gulf itself... particularly a country like Iran which was already facing very, very high food inflation.
moments.why: L'expert analyse l'impact des pénuries alimentaires et de l'inflation sur les pays de la région dont l'Iran.

moments.quote: It is difficult just because we don't know how long this will um persist and and, you know, if if this is resolved relatively quickly, then then I think the impacts will be fair would be modest, but the longer this is prolonged and the the more length of time that that energy prices remain remain above $100 and oil prices remain above $100 a barrel and um you know, I think that there we will begin to see uh some inflation threat. How much of it really ends up in food inflation?
moments.why: L'expert discute de l'impact à long terme de la crise sur l'inflation des denrées alimentaires en fonction de la durée du conflit.

videos.title: Could the war on Iran pose lasting risks to global food security? | Inside Story

moments.quote: While some countries have stored more fertilizer after the Ukraine war threatened supplies, the timing of the current disruption comes at a critical time for many farmers. In the Northern Hemisphere, spring planting generally runs from mid-February to early May, but continued disruption to fertilizer supplies would likely create lower yield for staple crops. And that would lead to higher prices with the United Nations warning that means more risk to food security, especially for poorer or more vulnerable countries.
moments.why: Le journaliste explique que la guerre en Ukraine puis les interruptions actuelles de fertilisants font courir de graves risques sur la sécurité alimentaire mondiale.

moments.quote: Well, it's both the volume of the reduction in fertilizer throughput through the Strait, as the item said 30% of the world's fertilizer passes through the Strait, which has now been disrupted for over a month... and that means that unless countries have got fertilizer stocks worth two or three or six months or a year's worth... they are going to be hit at some point when the buffer stocks run out.
moments.why: L'expert avertit des risques de famine et de crise alimentaire mondiale liés à la pénurie de fertilisants provoquée par la guerre.
